units.en: Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, a Carthaginian.
If it is true — and no one doubts it —
that the Roman people surpassed every nation in courage,
then it cannot be denied that Hannibal outstripped every other commander in skill by just as great a margin
as the Roman people exceed all nations in bravery.
For as often as he engaged with the Romans in Italy,
he always came away the victor.
And had he not been weakened at home by the jealousy of his own countrymen,
he seems to have been able to defeat the Romans.
But the resentment of the many overpowered the courage of one man.
Yet he kept alive the hatred of his father towards the Romans, handed down to him almost as an inheritance,
so faithfully that he laid down his life sooner than he laid down that hatred;
indeed, even once he had been driven from his homeland and depended on the resources of others,
he never once stopped waging war on Rome, at least in spirit.
For, to pass over Philip, whom Hannibal turned into Rome's enemy from a distance,
King Antiochus was, in those days, the most powerful ruler of all.
Hannibal inflamed him with so great a desire for war
that he attempted to bring his forces against Italy all the way from the Red Sea.
When Roman envoys came to Antiochus's court
to sound out his intentions and to work through secret schemes
to make the king suspicious of Hannibal,
as though he had been bribed by them and now thought differently than before —
and their scheme did not fail, and Hannibal found out about it,
and realised he was being shut out of the king's inner counsels —
he went to the king as soon as the chance arose,
and after reminding him at length of his loyalty and his hatred of Rome,
he added this: 'My father
Hamilcar,' he said, 'when I was a small boy, no more than nine years old,
as he was setting out from Carthage for Spain as commander-in-chief,
offered sacrifice to Jupiter, greatest and best of the gods.'
'While that sacred rite was being carried out, he asked me whether I wanted to go with him to the camp.
When I gladly agreed and began to beg him not to hesitate to take me, he said,
"I will — if you give me the pledge I ask for." He then led me to the altar
where he had begun the sacrifice, and, sending everyone else away, made me hold it and swear that I would never be
a friend to Rome.
That oath, given to my father, I have kept right up to this day so completely that no one should doubt
I will remain of the same mind for whatever time is left to me.
So if you plan anything friendly towards Rome, you will not be acting unwisely if you keep it from me; but when
you prepare for war, you will only cheat yourself if you do not put me in command of it.' It was at that
age, then, as I have said, that he set out for Spain with his father.
After his death, Hasdrubal took over as commander, and Hannibal was put in charge of the whole cavalry.
When Hasdrubal too was killed, the army handed him supreme command, and this was publicly
approved once word reached Carthage.
So it was that Hannibal, not yet twenty-five, became commander, and within the next
three years subdued every people of Spain by war; he took Saguntum, an ally of Rome, by
storm, and raised three very large armies.
One of these he sent to Africa, a second he left with his brother Hasdrubal in Spain, and the third he took
with him into Italy. He crossed the Pyrenean pass, and wherever his march took him he fought every people he met,
letting no one go free unless defeated.
When he reached the Alps, which separate Italy from Gaul — mountains no army had ever crossed
before him except that of the Greek Hercules, which is why the pass is still called the Graian Pass
today — he cut down the Alpine tribes who tried to stop his crossing, opened up the terrain, built roads, and made it possible
for a fully laden elephant to travel where, before, a single unarmed man could barely crawl. By this route
he brought his forces across and reached Italy.
He had already fought the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio at the Rhone and driven him back; with this
same man he fought again at Clastidium on the Po, and sent him off wounded and routed.
A third time this same Scipio, now with his colleague Tiberius Longus, met him at the Trebia;
Hannibal engaged them both and crushed them. From there he crossed the Apennines through the territory of the Ligurians,
making for Etruria.
On this march he was struck by such a severe eye infection that afterwards he never had
the full use of his right eye again. While still suffering from this and being carried in a litter, he ambushed and destroyed the consul Gaius Flaminius
and his army at Lake Trasimene, and not long after that
the praetor Gaius Centenius, along with his picked troops holding the mountain passes.
From here he reached Apulia, where the two consuls, Gaius Terentius and Lucius Aemilius, came out to meet him.
In a single battle he put both their armies to flight, killed the consul Paulus, and several ex-consuls
besides, among them Gnaeus Servilius Geminus, who had been consul the year before.
After fighting this battle he set out for Rome, unopposed. He waited for some days in the hills near the city,
and, having camped there, was on his way back to Capua when Quintus Fabius
Maximus, the Roman dictator, blocked his path in Falernian territory.
Trapped by the narrowness of the terrain, Hannibal got his army out that night without a single loss, and tricked Fabius
— for all his skill as a commander. For, under cover of darkness, he had bundles of twigs tied to the horns
of young cattle and set alight, then sent a great many of these animals scattering across the hillside.
By presenting this sudden sight he struck such terror into the Roman army that not one man dared go beyond
the rampart.
Not many days after this, he lured Marcus Minucius Rufus — the Master of Horse, holding power equal
to the dictator's — into battle by a trick, and routed him. He destroyed Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus,
consul for the second time, by luring him into an ambush in Lucania while Hannibal himself was elsewhere, and killed Marcus Claudius Marcellus,
five times consul, near Venusia in much the same way.
It would take too long to list every battle. So this one fact will be enough to show
how great a man he was: as long as he remained in Italy, no one stood against him in open battle, and no one
pitched camp against him in the open field after Cannae.
From here, still undefeated, he was called home to defend his own country, and made war against Publius Scipio, the son of the man
whom he himself had already routed first at the Rhone, again at the Po, and a third time at the Trebia.
With his homeland's resources by now exhausted, he wanted to settle the war with him for the time being, so as
to fight again later from a stronger position. A meeting took place, but no terms were agreed.
A few days after that meeting he fought this same Scipio at Zama. Beaten there, he covered — incredible as it sounds —
the distance to Hadrumetum, some three hundred miles
from Zama, in two days and two nights.
During this retreat the Numidians who had left the battlefield alongside him ambushed him; not only
did he escape them, he overpowered them in turn. At Hadrumetum he gathered the survivors of the retreat, and within a few
days, through fresh recruitment, had assembled a large force once more.
While he was throwing himself into these preparations, the Carthaginians made peace with Rome.
He nonetheless remained in command of the army afterwards and carried on operations in Africa, as did
his brother Mago, right up until the consulship of Publius Sulpicius and Gaius Aurelius.
For in their term of office, Carthaginian envoys came to Rome to thank the senate and people
of Rome for making peace with them, and to present them with a golden crown for it,
while also asking that their hostages might live at Fregellae, and that their prisoners be returned.
The senate's reply was this: their gift was welcome and accepted; the hostages
could stay wherever they had requested; but the prisoners would not be returned, because the Carthaginians still kept Hannibal — the man responsible
for starting the war, and Rome's bitterest enemy — in command of
an army, along with his brother Mago.
Once the Carthaginians learned of this reply, they recalled Hannibal and Mago home. As soon as he
returned, Hannibal was made “king” (that is, suffete), in the twenty-second year after he had first become general. For just as Rome
elected consuls, so Carthage elected a pair of kings every year.
In that office Hannibal applied himself with exactly the same energy he had shown in war.
For, through new revenues, he made sure there was not only enough money to pay what was owed to Rome under the treaty, but
also a surplus left over to store in the treasury.
Then, in the consulship of Marcus Claudius and Lucius Furius, envoys came from Rome to Carthage.
Believing they had been sent to demand his surrender, Hannibal boarded a ship in secret, before they could even be granted an audience with the senate,
and fled to Syria and King Antiochus.
Once this became known, the Carthaginians sent two ships to arrest him if they could catch him,
confiscated his property, tore his house down to its foundations,
and declared him an exile.
In the third year after fleeing his home, in the consulship of Lucius Cornelius and Quintus Minucius,
Hannibal reached Africa with five ships, in the territory of Cyrene, to see whether he might draw the Carthaginians into
Antiochus's war by holding out the promise of his support — Antiochus he had already persuaded to invade
Italy with his forces. He summoned his brother Mago to join him there.
As soon as the Carthaginians learned of this, they punished Mago in his absence exactly as they had punished Hannibal.
Their situation now hopeless, the two brothers set sail, and Hannibal reached
Antiochus. Two different accounts survive of Mago's death: some record that he died in a shipwreck, others that he was killed
by his own slaves.
As for Antiochus, if he had been as willing to follow Hannibal's advice in fighting the war as he had been in undertaking it,
he would have fought for supreme power nearer the Tiber than at Thermopylae. Yet even when
he could see the king pursuing many foolish schemes, Hannibal never once abandoned him.
He commanded a few ships, which he had been ordered to bring from Syria to Asia, and with these he fought
the fleet of Rhodes in the Pamphylian Sea. In that battle, though his side was beaten by the greater numbers of the enemy,
on the wing where he himself fought, he came out on top.
Once Antiochus had been defeated, Hannibal, fearing he might be handed over — which would certainly have happened had he ever put himself in Roman hands —
came to the Gortynians in Crete, to consider from there where he might go next.
But this shrewdest of all men could see he would be in great danger, unless he took precautions,
because of the Cretans' greed: he was carrying a large sum of money with him, and he knew
word of it had already spread.
So he devised the following plan. He filled several jars with lead and covered the tops with gold and
silver. These he deposited, in front of the leading citizens, in the temple of Diana, pretending he was entrusting his fortune
to their good faith. With them thoroughly deceived, he then filled bronze statues he had been carrying with him with all his
actual money, and left these lying casually in the open courtyard of his house.
The people of Gortyn guarded the temple with great care — not so much against anyone else as against Hannibal himself,
in case he should try to remove his own property without their knowledge and take it away with him.
Having saved his fortune in this way, and having made fools of every Cretan, Hannibal reached
King Prusias in Pontus. At his court he kept exactly the same attitude towards Italy, and did nothing else but arm and
train the king against Rome.
Seeing that Prusias lacked the resources to stand on his own, Hannibal won over other kings to his side
and drew warlike nations into alliance with him. Eumenes, king of Pergamum, a close ally of Rome,
was at odds with Prusias, and war was being fought between them on both land and sea;
but on both fronts Eumenes had the advantage, thanks to his alliance with Rome. This only made Hannibal
more determined to see him crushed — if he could remove Eumenes, he reasoned, everything else would come more easily.
To kill him, he devised the following plan.
Within a few days the two sides were due to fight it out at sea. Hannibal was outnumbered in ships, and would have to fight
by trickery, since he could not match his enemy in strength. He ordered as many live venomous snakes as possible
to be gathered and packed into earthenware pots.
Once he had collected a great number of these, on the very day set for the naval battle,
he called his marines together and gave the order: all of them were to converge on the one ship carrying King Eumenes,
while against everyone else they need only defend themselves: thanks to the great number of snakes, he told them, they would easily
manage this.
He would make sure they knew which ship the king himself was sailing on; if they either captured or
killed him, he promised they would be richly rewarded.
With his men encouraged in this way, the two fleets moved out to fight. Once the battle lines
were drawn up, and before the signal for battle was given, Hannibal, wanting his own side to know exactly where
Eumenes was, sent a messenger out in a small boat carrying a herald's staff.
When the man reached the enemy ships and, holding up a letter, announced that he was looking
for the king, he was taken straight to Eumenes, since no one doubted the letter contained some offer
of peace. Once the messenger had pointed out the commander's ship to his own side, he returned the way he had come.
But when Eumenes opened the letter, he found nothing in it except words meant to mock him.
Though he was baffled by this and could find no explanation for it, he still did not hesitate to
join battle at once.
As the two sides clashed, the Bithynians, on Hannibal's orders, all together attacked Eumenes's ship.
Unable to withstand their assault, the king sought safety in flight, and would not have escaped
had he not taken shelter within his own defences, positioned on the nearby shore.
As the other Pergamene ships were pressing their opponents harder, the earthenware pots I mentioned
earlier suddenly started being hurled onto their ships. At first these missiles only drew laughter from the fighting men,
who could not work out why this was being done.
But once they saw their ships filling with snakes, they were thrown into total panic at this new form of attack, and,
unable to tell which danger to avoid, they turned their ships around and fled back
to their own naval camp.
In this way Hannibal defeated the Pergamene fleet through strategy — and not only on this occasion, but often on other occasions too,
he drove back his enemies on land with the same cunning.
While these events were unfolding in Asia, it happened by chance that envoys of Prusias were dining in Rome with
the ex-consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus, and when Hannibal's name came up in conversation, one of them mentioned
that he was living in Prusias's kingdom.
Flamininus reported this to the senate the next day. The senators, who felt they would never be free
of plots as long as Hannibal lived, sent envoys to Bithynia — Flamininus among them —
to ask the king not to keep Rome's bitterest enemy at his court, but to hand him over. Prusias did not dare
refuse them outright,
but he did object to one thing: they should not demand that he himself do something that was against the laws of hospitality. Let them arrest him themselves, he said, if they could;
they would easily find the place where he was. For Hannibal stayed in
one place, in a fortress that the king had given him as a gift, which he had built in such a way
that he had exits on every side of the building, clearly afraid that what actually happened might come about.
When the Roman envoys reached the place and surrounded his house with a large body of troops, a boy
watching from the doorway told Hannibal that an unusual number of armed men were appearing. Hannibal
ordered him to go around every door of the building and quickly report back whether it was surrounded
on every side in the same way.
When the boy had quickly reported what the situation was and shown that every exit was blocked, Hannibal realised
this had not happened by chance, but that he himself was the target, and that he should no longer keep his life. So as not to lose it
at the will of another, and mindful of his past courage, he took the poison he always kept
with him.
So this bravest of men, after enduring so many different hardships, found peace at last in his seventieth year.
Under which consuls he died is a matter of dispute: Atticus, in his own Annals, records his death under
the consulship of Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Quintus Fabius Labeo; Polybius, under Lucius Aemilius Paulus
and Gnaeus Baebius Tamphilus; Sulpicius Blitho, under Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus.

essays.q: how does Nepos make this a powerful introduction to Hannibal?
points: Nepos opens like an entry in a list (name, father, nation), at once naming Hamilcar and Carthage
he praises Hannibal as the greatest of all generals, a bold claim for a Roman audience
he protects Roman pride by giving Rome courage and Hannibal skill, so the praise does not insult his readers
Hannibal was never beaten in Italy, and Nepos implies he would have won the war
his downfall is blamed on jealousy at home, which makes him a tragic figure betrayed by his own people
the hatred of Rome is presented as an inheritance from his father, part of his identity
the chapter ends with Hannibal still fighting Rome in spirit even in exile, which looks ahead to the rest of the Life
features: Hannibal, Hamilcaris filius, Carthaginiensis: the bare opening, like an entry in a list (name, father, nation), introduces Hannibal at once through the father whose hatred he inherits, and ends on Carthaginiensis to mark him as Rome’s great enemy
si verum est, quod nemo dubitat: the parenthesis assures Roman readers of their own supremacy before the bold claim that follows, so the praise of Hannibal carries more weight
non est infitiandum: litotes makes the praise sound undeniable, as if the facts force Nepos to admit Hannibal’s greatness

tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes: the balanced tanto … quanto comparison ranks Hannibal above all generals as high as Rome stands above all nations, a powerful claim for an opening
quotienscumque cum eo congressus est in Italia, semper discessit superior: the sweeping quotienscumque … semper allows no exception, and the sentence ends emphatically on superior

quod nisi domi civium suorum invidia debilitatus esset, Romanos videtur superare potuisse: the unreal condition imagines Hannibal defeating Rome, softened by the cautious videtur, which makes his failure tragic
multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem: the antithesis of many against one, and spite against courage, sums up his fate in one short, pointed sentence
velut hereditate relictum odium paternum: the metaphor of an inheritance makes hatred of Rome part of Hannibal’s identity from the start
ut prius animam quam id deposuerit: hyperbole: he would give up his life sooner than his hatred, which shows its power over him
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis: the emphatic numquam ends the introduction on his unbroken war with Rome, preparing for the rest of the Life

essays.q: how does Nepos praise Hannibal while keeping his Roman readers on his side?
points: he begins by granting that Rome surpassed every nation in courage, a point no one doubts
his praise of Hannibal is presented as a fact that cannot be denied, so it seems forced on him
Hannibal is given skill and judgement, Rome courage, so neither side is insulted
Hannibal was never beaten in Italy, a bold claim, softened by the cautious ‘seems’
his defeat is blamed on jealousy at home, so Rome’s victory does not have to be explained away
the hatred he inherited from his father makes him a formidable but understandable enemy
even in exile he never stopped fighting Rome, which shows how dangerous he remained
features: si verum est, quod nemo dubitat: the conditional opening and the parenthesis concede Rome’s superiority first, so Roman readers are reassured before Hannibal is praised
ut populus Romanus omnes gentes virtute superarit: Rome is said to surpass all peoples in courage, flattering the readers and setting the standard for the comparison
non est infitiandum: litotes presents the praise as reluctant but forced by the facts, so Nepos seems fair rather than disloyal

tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes: the careful balance gives Hannibal prudentia and Rome fortitudo, so each side has its own virtue and Hannibal is never braver than the Romans
semper discessit superior: the strong claim of unbroken victory is confined to battles in Italy, a precise limit that keeps the praise defensible
Romanos videtur superare potuisse: the cautious videtur and the unreal condition soften the idea of a Roman defeat
domi civium suorum invidia debilitatus: Hannibal is beaten by the jealousy of his own people, so Rome’s honour is not damaged by his downfall
multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem: the antithesis praises his virtus while placing the blame at Carthage
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis: the closing emphasis on his lifelong hostility reminds Roman readers that this great man was their enemy

features: multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem: the antithesis shows Hannibal undone by others’ spite, so his own hatred of Rome stands out as the constant in his life
velut hereditate relictum odium paternum erga Romanos: the inheritance metaphor makes the hatred something he was born into, the force behind everything he does
sic conservavit, ut prius animam quam id deposuerit: the result clause and the hyperbole of giving up his life before his hatred show it outlasting everything else
cum patria pulsus esset et alienarum opum indigeret: the pair of hardships, exile and dependence, stresses that nothing could weaken his hostility
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis: the emphatic negative and animo show him at war with Rome in his mind even when he had no army
ut omittam Philippum, quem absens hostem reddidit Romanis: praeteritio still names Philip, and absens shows his hatred working even at a distance
omnium iis temporibus potentissimus rex Antiochus: the superlative and the delayed name make the king he turns against Rome as great as possible
hunc tanta cupiditate incendit bellandi: the fire metaphor in incendit presents Hannibal as the spark that sets kings alight with war
usque a rubro mari arma conatus sit inferre Italiae: the geographical extremes, ending on Italiae, show his hatred driving a war across the world towards Rome

consiliis clandestinis ut Hannibalem in suspicionem regi adducerent: the alliteration of c and the secret plotting show how much the Romans fear him

neque id frustra fecissent idque Hannibal comperisset seque ab interioribus consiliis segregari vidisset: polysyndeton builds up the stages of the plot and his discovery of it, so his response comes as a climax

puerulo me, utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato: the diminutive and the precise age make the boy vivid and stress how young he was

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s account of his oath persuasive?

id cum libenter accepissem atque ab eo petere coepissem ne dubitaret ducere: the boy’s eagerness persuades the king that hatred of Rome was Hannibal’s own choice from the start

non imprudenter feceris, si me celaris: litotes shows the tact of a leader handling a king
te ipsum frustraberis, si non me in eo principem posueris: he tells a king bluntly that he would be fooling himself, and ends his speech on principem, a claim to command
hac igitur, qua diximus, aetate cum patre in Hispaniam profectus est: Nepos rounds off the story and returns to the start of his career at the age of nine
cuius post obitum, Hasdrubale imperatore suffecto, equitatui omni praefuit: the compressed ablative absolutes move quickly to his first command, of all the cavalry
hoc quoque interfecto exercitus summam imperii ad eum detulit: the army itself chooses him for supreme command, a sign of a natural leader
id Carthaginem delatum publice comprobatum est: the repetition of detulit … delatum links the soldiers’ choice to its official approval, showing that his leadership was recognised by all

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as an exceptional commander?
points: Hannibal becomes supreme commander before the age of twenty-five
within three years he conquers all the peoples of Spain
he takes Saguntum, an allied state, by force
he raises three huge armies and plans on a grand scale, sending them to Africa, Spain and Italy
on the march no people he meets escapes defeat
he crosses the Alps, which no army had crossed before except Hercules’, so his feat is set beside a legend
he defeats the Alpine tribes and builds a road where an elephant can pass, which shows practical skill as well as courage
features: sic Hannibal minor quinque et viginti annis natus imperator factus: the precise detail of his age stresses how young he was to command
proximo triennio omnes gentes Hispaniae bello subegit: the hyperbole of omnes and the short time span stress the speed and scale of his conquests
Saguntum, foederatam civitatem, vi expugnavit, tres exercitus maximos comparavit: asyndeton piles up his achievements, and the superlative maximos adds to their scale

ex his unum in Africam misit, alterum cum Hasdrubale fratre in Hispania reliquit, tertium in Italiam secum duxit: the tricolon unum … alterum … tertium shows a commander planning on three fronts at once, climaxing in Italy
quacumque iter fecit, cum omnibus incolis conflixit: neminem nisi victum dimisit: the sweeping quacumque and omnibus and the emphatic negative neminem allow no exception to his victories
quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat: the double negative nemo umquam and the comparison with Hercules raise his feat to heroic level
Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit: the strong verb concidit shows how he cut down all opposition
loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit: the asyndeton of short verbs conveys his energy and his skill as an engineer

ut ea elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere: the contrast of a fully equipped elephant with a single unarmed man who could barely crawl shows the scale of what he achieved

essays.lemma: ex his unum … in Italiamque pervenit
essays.q: how does Nepos make the crossing of the Alps seem a heroic achievement?
points: Hannibal leads the third army into Italy himself
he crosses the Pyrenees and defeats every people on the way
the Alps are a great natural barrier between Gaul and Italy
only Hercules had crossed them with an army before
he cuts down the Alpine tribes who try to stop him
he opens up the land and builds roads
a laden elephant can now go where an unarmed man could barely crawl
features: tertium in Italiam secum duxit: the climax of the tricolon of armies places Italy and Hannibal’s own march at the centre of the story
saltum Pyrenaeum transiit: the bare statement of crossing the Pyrenees makes a great feat sound routine, preparing for the greater one
neminem nisi victum dimisit: the emphatic negative shows him conquering all who stood in his way
quae Italiam ab Gallia seiungunt: the Alps are presented as a barrier dividing nations, raising the stakes of the crossing
quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat: the double negative and the comparison with Hercules make the crossing heroic and nearly unique
quo facto is hodie saltus Graius appellatur: the reference to the pass still bearing the hero’s name gives the achievement a legendary quality
Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit: the vivid verb concidit shows him cutting down the tribes who resisted
loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit: asyndeton of three short verbs conveys relentless effort

elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere: the contrast of a laden elephant with one unarmed man barely crawling, stressed by vix and repere, shows how hard the route had been
hac copias traduxit in Italiamque pervenit: the short closing sentence marks the achievement of the goal

essays.q: how does Nepos convey the speed of Hannibal’s rise and his early successes?
points: two commanders die in quick succession, dealt with in a few words
Hannibal is given the cavalry, then the supreme command
the army chooses him and the state approves
he is not yet twenty-five
he conquers all of Spain within three years
he takes Saguntum and raises three huge armies
he crosses the Pyrenees and defeats everyone in his way
features: cuius post obitum, Hasdrubale imperatore suffecto, equitatui omni praefuit: the compressed ablative absolutes pass quickly over events, so his first command arrives almost at once
hoc quoque interfecto exercitus summam imperii ad eum detulit: another brief ablative absolute moves straight to his supreme command
id Carthaginem delatum publice comprobatum est: the short sentence shows Carthage confirming his appointment without delay
minor quinque et viginti annis natus imperator factus: the precise age stresses how young he was when he took command
proximo triennio omnes gentes Hispaniae bello subegit: the short time span and omnes convey the speed and sweep of his conquest of Spain
Saguntum, foederatam civitatem, vi expugnavit, tres exercitus maximos comparavit: asyndeton lists achievements rapidly, one after another
ex his unum in Africam misit, alterum cum Hasdrubale fratre in Hispania reliquit, tertium in Italiam secum duxit: the brisk tricolon shows armies dispatched in quick succession
saltum Pyrenaeum transiit, quacumque iter fecit, cum omnibus incolis conflixit: short clauses in asyndeton keep the march moving at speed
neminem nisi victum dimisit: the emphatic negative closes the passage on unbroken success

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s victories in Italy seem overwhelming?
points: the same Roman commander, Scipio, is beaten again and again, at the Rhone, the Po and the Trebia
Scipio is sent away wounded and in flight, a humiliating picture of a Roman consul
two consuls together at the Trebia are crushed at once
Hannibal is struck by an eye disease, yet wins even while carried in a litter
he destroys Flaminius and his army at Trasimene by an ambush, and soon afterwards Centenius and his picked troops
in Apulia both consular armies are routed in a single battle
the list of the dead rises from a consul to several ex-consuls, showing how much of Rome’s leadership was lost
features: conflixerat apud Rhodanum cum P. Cornelio Scipione consule eumque pepulerat: the first victory over a consul is told in a single brisk sentence, setting the pattern of the chapter
cum hoc eodem Clastidi apud Padum decernit sauciumque inde ac fugatum dimittit: the historic present makes the second victory vivid, and the paired participles show the same consul wounded and routed
tertio idem Scipio cum collega Tiberio Longo apud Trebiam adversus eum venit: tertio and idem stress that the same enemy kept coming back to be beaten
cum his manum conseruit, utrosque profligavit: asyndeton and the strong verb profligavit make the victory over both commanders sound instant and total
qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur: even ill and carried in a litter he wins, which makes his victories seem all the more overwhelming
C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit: a consul and his whole army are trapped and killed in one sentence
neque multo post C. Centenium praetorem cum delecta manu saltus occupantem: neque multo post adds another victory in quick succession
utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit: the contrast of two armies with a single battle shows the scale of the victory at Cannae
Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares, in his Cn. Servilium Geminum, qui superiore anno fuerat consul: the list of slain consuls and ex-consuls builds to a climax of Roman losses

essays.q: how does Nepos present the Roman commanders who face Hannibal?
points: Scipio fights Hannibal again and again and is beaten each time
Scipio is left wounded and in flight, a humiliating image for a consul
even two consuls together at the Trebia are crushed
Flaminius falls into an ambush and dies with his army
Centenius and his picked troops are destroyed
in Apulia both consuls come out together against Hannibal
Paulus and several ex-consuls are killed, so a whole layer of Rome’s leadership is lost
features: cum P. Cornelio Scipione consule eumque pepulerat: the consul is named in full and then simply driven back, his rank making his defeat more striking
sauciumque inde ac fugatum dimittit: the paired participles show the same consul wounded and put to flight, and dimittit suggests Hannibal letting him go at will
tertio idem Scipio cum collega Tiberio Longo apud Trebiam adversus eum venit: tertio idem makes Scipio return for a third defeat, persistent but unsuccessful
cum his manum conseruit, utrosque profligavit: the two commanders are crushed together in two short clauses
C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit: the consul falls into an ambush with his army, outwitted and killed
C. Centenium praetorem cum delecta manu saltus occupantem: even a praetor with a picked force holding the pass is overcome
ibi obviam ei venerunt duo consules, C. Terentius et L. Aemilius: the two consuls are named as they march out to meet him, building expectation
utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit: the contrast between two consular armies and one battle shows the commanders’ helplessness
Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares: the list of fallen consuls and ex-consuls presents the Roman leadership as repeatedly beaten, however senior its men

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal seem both human and unstoppable?
points: he presses on over the Apennines towards Etruria
he is struck by a severe eye disease
he never again has the full use of his right eye
still ill and carried in a litter, he ambushes and kills the consul Flaminius and his army
soon after he destroys Centenius and his picked troops
in Apulia he routs the armies of both consuls in a single battle
he kills the consul Paulus and several ex-consuls
features: inde per Ligures Appenninum transiit, petens Etruriam: another mountain range is crossed in a single clause, as if nothing could stop him
hoc itinere adeo gravi morbo afficitur oculorum: the historic present and adeo gravi make his illness vivid and show his human weakness
ut postea numquam dextro aeque bene usus sit: the result clause and numquam stress a lasting injury, the cost of the campaign to him
qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur: the image of the general carried in a litter shows how ill he was, making what follows more remarkable
C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit: straight after the litter comes the ambush and death of a consul and his army, so the sick man is still unstoppable
neque multo post C. Centenium praetorem cum delecta manu saltus occupantem: neque multo post adds another quick victory
hinc in Apuliam pervenit: the short sentence keeps the advance moving
utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit: the contrast of two armies and one battle shows his overwhelming power
Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares: the climax of Roman losses ends the passage on his unstoppable success

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a master of cunning?
points: Hannibal seems trapped by the narrow terrain, yet escapes at night without losing a man
he deceives Fabius, who is described as the cleverest of commanders
the trick with burning brushwood tied to the horns of cattle is described in vivid detail
the sudden sight terrifies a whole Roman army into staying behind its rampart
he lures Minucius into battle by a trick and routs him
he destroys Gracchus and Marcellus by ambushes, even without being present himself
Nepos ends by claiming no one could face him in open battle, so cunning and strength combine to make him unbeatable in Italy
features: hic clausus locorum angustiis noctu sine ullo detrimento exercitus se expedivit: the trap and the escape without any loss are set side by side, so his cunning gets him out of an impossible position
Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba: the superlative praises Fabius as the cleverest of commanders in the very clause where Hannibal fools him, so Hannibal seems cleverer still
obducta nocte sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit: the vivid detail of burning brushwood tied to the cattle’s horns shows an ingenious trick
eiusque generis multitudinem magnam dispalatam immisit: the great scattered herd shows the scale of the deception
quo repentino visu obiecto tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum: repentino and tantum terrorem stress the sudden fear his trick causes
ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus: the result clause ends on nemo sit ausus: a whole Roman army is pinned down by a trick
M. Minucium Rufum, magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, dolo productum in proelium fugavit: dolo productum shows him luring a senior commander into battle by deceit
Ti. Sempronium Gracchum, iterum consulem, in Lucanis absens in insidias inductum sustulit: absens shows his cunning working even at a distance
M. Claudium Marcellum, quinquies consulem, apud Venusiam pari modo interfecit: pari modo makes ambush his signature method
nemo ei in acie restitit, nemo adversus eum post Cannensem pugnam in campo castra posuit: the anaphora of nemo shows that the Romans no longer dared to face him

essays.lemma: hac pugna pugnata … nemo sit ausus
essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s dealings with Fabius dramatic?
points: after the battle Hannibal marches on Rome unopposed and camps in the hills near the city
Fabius, the dictator, is given his full name and title as a serious opponent
Hannibal appears trapped in narrow ground
he escapes at night without losing a man
Fabius, the most cunning of commanders, is himself deceived
the strange night-time trick with burning brushwood on the horns of cattle
the sudden sight terrifies the Romans so that no one leaves the rampart
features: hac pugna pugnata Romam profectus est nullo resistente: the ablative absolutes and nullo resistente show Hannibal marching on Rome unopposed, raising the tension
in propinquis urbi montibus moratus est: the image of him waiting in the hills near the city keeps the threat hanging over Rome
Q. Fabius Maximus, dictator Romanus, in agro Falerno ei se obiecit: the full name and title build up Fabius as a formidable opponent, and se obiecit shows him blocking the way
hic clausus locorum angustiis: the trap in the narrow ground creates a dramatic crisis
noctu sine ullo detrimento exercitus se expedivit: the sudden escape by night without any loss resolves the crisis at once
Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba: the irony of the cleverest commander being fooled adds to the drama
obducta nocte sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit: the vivid picture of blazing brushwood on cattle’s horns in the dark makes the scene striking
quo repentino visu obiecto tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum: the sudden sight and the great terror show the effect on the watching Romans
ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus: the episode ends on the paralysed Roman army, the climax of Hannibal’s trick

essays.q: how does Nepos convince the reader of Hannibal’s greatness as a general?
points: he lures Minucius into battle by a trick, though Minucius has power equal to the dictator’s
he destroys Gracchus, twice consul, by an ambush without being present
he kills Marcellus, five times consul, in the same way
his victims grow steadily more senior
Nepos says it would take too long to list every battle
one fact is said to be enough to prove his greatness
no one stood against him in battle in Italy, and after Cannae no one camped against him
features: M. Minucium Rufum, magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, dolo productum in proelium fugavit: the rank of each defeated Roman is given in full, so every victory is over a great commander
Ti. Sempronium Gracchum, iterum consulem: iterum consulem stresses the experience of the man he destroys
in Lucanis absens in insidias inductum sustulit: absens shows him defeating a consul without even being there
M. Claudium Marcellum, quinquies consulem, apud Venusiam pari modo interfecit: the climax of the list is a five-times consul, killed in the same way
longum est omnia enumerare proelia: Nepos claims there are too many battles to list, implying that his victories are countless
quare hoc unum satis erit dictum, ex quo intellegi possit, quantus ille fuerit: hoc unum and quantus ille introduce one decisive fact as proof of his greatness
quamdiu in Italia fuit, nemo ei in acie restitit: the sweeping quamdiu and nemo cover his whole time in Italy
nemo adversus eum post Cannensem pugnam in campo castra posuit: the anaphora of nemo builds to the claim that no Roman dared even to camp against him in open country

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal in a positive light even in defeat?
points: he leaves Italy undefeated and is recalled to defend his country, which makes him a patriot
Nepos reminds us that he had beaten Scipio’s father three times
the need for peace is put down to Carthage’s exhausted resources
even his attempt at peace is a plan to fight again later from a stronger position
the defeat at Zama is passed over in a single word
Nepos marvels at his retreat of three hundred miles in two days and nights
he escapes and crushes the Numidians who ambush him
within a few days he has raised a large army again, so the chapter ends with his recovery
features: hinc invictus patriam defensum revocatus: invictus stands first, so Hannibal leaves Italy unbeaten; the supine of purpose defensum shows him called home to defend his country, which presents him as a patriot answering its call

quem ipse primo apud Rhodanum, iterum apud Padum, tertio apud Trebiam fugarat: the numbered tricolon (primo, iterum, tertio) recalls three victories over the Scipios just as he faces the son, so the reader remembers his strength before the defeat
exhaustis iam patriae facultatibus: the ablative absolute gives Carthage’s exhausted resources as the reason for seeking peace, which moves the blame for what follows away from Hannibal

cupivit impraesentiarum bellum componere, quo valentior postea congrederetur: the purpose clause shows that even his wish for peace is a plan to fight again from strength, so he remains the determined general
apud Zamam cum eodem conflixit: pulsus: understatement: the decisive defeat of the war is told in a single participle, so Nepos hurries past Hannibal’s one great loss
incredibile dictu: the narrator’s own exclamation of wonder turns the reader’s attention from the defeat to an astonishing feat
biduo et duabus noctibus … milia passuum trecenta: precise figures of time and distance make the retreat sound measured and real, and so all the more impressive
quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit: non solum … sed etiam builds to a climax: escaping the ambush would have been enough, yet he crushes his attackers too
novis dilectibus paucis diebus multos contraxit: the contrast of paucis with multos, and contraxit as the final word, close the chapter on his swift recovery

essays.q: how does Nepos make this passage fast-moving and vivid?
points: the story moves from Italy to Africa in a single sentence
the peace talks are dismissed in two short clauses
the defeat at Zama is told in one word
the retreat is astonishingly fast, with exact times and distances
his own companions in flight suddenly ambush him
he escapes and crushes them
within a few days he has a large army again
features: hinc invictus patriam defensum revocatus bellum gessit: four compressed phrases carry Hannibal from Italy to war in Africa within one clause, which sets a rapid pace from the start
primo apud Rhodanum, iterum apud Padum, tertio apud Trebiam: the brisk numbered tricolon races through three earlier victories in a handful of words
in colloquium convenit; condiciones non convenerunt: two short clauses in asyndeton, with wordplay on convenire, dispose of the peace talks bluntly and quickly
post id factum paucis diebus apud Zamam cum eodem conflixit: the time phrase hurries the narrative straight on to the decisive battle
conflixit: pulsus: the battle and the defeat follow each other in two words, so the climax of the war flashes past
incredibile dictu: Nepos breaks in with his own astonishment, a vivid personal reaction that draws the reader in
biduo et duabus noctibus Hadrumetum pervenit, quod abest ab Zama circiter milia passuum trecenta: exact times and the huge distance make the speed of the flight concrete and vivid
Numidae, qui simul cum eo ex acie excesserant, insidiati sunt ei: the sudden ambush by his own companions in flight adds a dramatic twist
quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit: the non solum … sed etiam climax gives a quick reversal, the hunted turning on the hunters
Hadrumeti reliquos e fuga collegit; novis dilectibus paucis diebus multos contraxit: two short main clauses in asyndeton, with paucis diebus, keep up the pace to the end

essays.lemma: post id factum … C. Aurelium consules
essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s energy and determination?
points: after his defeat at Zama he covers about three hundred miles in two days and two nights
he beats off and crushes the Numidians who ambush him
he gathers the survivors at Hadrumetum
he raises a large new army within a few days
he throws himself into preparations for more war
Carthage makes peace while he is still preparing
he nonetheless stays in command and carries on operations in Africa, with his brother Mago
features: apud Zamam cum eodem conflixit: pulsus: the defeat is passed over in one participle, so the emphasis falls on what Hannibal does next
incredibile dictu biduo et duabus noctibus Hadrumetum pervenit: the narrator’s wonder and the precise timing stress the astonishing energy of the retreat
quod abest ab Zama circiter milia passuum trecenta: the huge distance is held back to the end of the sentence, which emphasises his stamina
quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit: the climax shows his determination: even in flight he goes on the attack
Hadrumeti reliquos e fuga collegit: he gathers the survivors at once, which shows him refusing to accept defeat
novis dilectibus paucis diebus multos contraxit: the contrast of paucis with multos shows how quickly and energetically he rebuilds an army
cum in apparando acerrime esset occupatus: the superlative adverb acerrime shows him throwing all his energy into preparing for more war
Carthaginienses bellum cum Romanis composuerunt: Carthage’s peace is set against his preparations, so his determination stands out against his city’s surrender
ille nihilo setius exercitui postea praefuit resque in Africa gessit: nihilo setius (‘none the less’) and the emphatic ille stress that he carries on regardless, still in command

essays.q: how does Nepos show the growing gap between Hannibal and his own city?
points: Hannibal throws himself into preparing for war while Carthage makes peace
he carries on in command regardless, with his brother Mago beside him
Carthage humbly thanks Rome and sends a golden crown, eager to please the victor
the senate’s gracious reply turns into a sharp refusal, and the reason is Hannibal
Rome names him as the man who started the war and its bitterest enemy, so he becomes a problem for Carthage
Carthage obeys at once and recalls its two generals
even so he is given the highest office in the city, which Nepos explains by comparison with Rome’s consuls
features: cum in apparando acerrime esset occupatus, Carthaginienses bellum cum Romanis composuerunt: Hannibal’s furious preparations (the superlative acerrime) are set against his city making peace, the first sign of the split
ille nihilo setius exercitui postea praefuit: nihilo setius shows him carrying on as if the peace did not apply to him, so he and Carthage are pulling in different directions

qui senatui populoque Romano gratias agerent … corona aurea eos donarent simulque peterent: the sequence of thanking, giving and asking, with the golden crown, shows Carthage humbly courting Rome while its general still prepares for war
munus eorum gratum acceptumque esse: the gracious pair gratum acceptumque sets up the sharp refusal that follows

captivos non remissuros, quod Hannibalem … etiamnum cum imperio apud exercitum haberent: the refusal is pinned explicitly on Hannibal, so the city’s own general becomes the obstacle to its dealings with Rome
inimicissimum nomini Romano: the superlative brands Hannibal Rome’s worst enemy, a label Carthage cannot afford to ignore

hoc responso Carthaginienses cognito Hannibalem domum et Magonem revocarunt: Carthage obeys at once; the brisk main verb after the ablative absolute shows the city choosing Rome’s goodwill over its general

essays.q: how does Nepos present the Romans’ attitude towards Hannibal?
points: the senate accepts Carthage’s gift graciously
it grants the request about the hostages
it refuses to return the prisoners while Hannibal commands an army
it blames Hannibal personally for starting the war
it calls him the bitterest enemy of the Roman name
it is suspicious that he still holds a command, along with Mago
its reply alone is enough to make Carthage recall him
features: usque ad P. Sulpicium C. Aurelium consules: dating events by Rome’s consuls tells the story from Rome’s side, with Rome as the power that matters
his ex senatus consulto responsum est: the formal reference to a decree of the senate gives Rome’s answer official weight
munus eorum gratum acceptumque esse: indirect speech and the gracious pairing present a cool, courteous Rome accepting the gift
obsides, quo loco rogarent, futuros; captivos non remissuros: the balanced grant and refusal make the ‘no’ stand out: Rome gives way on the small matter only
quod Hannibalem, cuius opera susceptum bellum foret: Hannibal is named and blamed in the same breath, so Rome holds him personally responsible for the war
inimicissimum nomini Romano: the superlative and ‘the Roman name’ make him the enemy of everything Rome stands for

etiamnum cum imperio apud exercitum haberent itemque fratrem eius Magonem: etiamnum (‘even now’) shows Roman suspicion that the war is not over while he holds an army, and Mago is added as a further threat
hoc responso Carthaginienses cognito Hannibalem domum et Magonem revocarunt: Rome’s words alone are enough to have him recalled, which shows the weight of Roman hostility

essays.q: how does Nepos show Carthage’s weakness in its dealings with Rome after the war?
points: Carthaginian envoys come to Rome to thank the Romans for making peace
they present a golden crown
they ask favours humbly, about their hostages and prisoners
the senate grants one request and refuses the other
the refusal is based on Carthage’s own general
Carthage obeys at once and recalls Hannibal and Mago
even Carthage’s highest office is explained by comparison with Rome’s
features: legati Carthaginienses Romam venerunt, qui senatui populoque Romano gratias agerent: Carthage sends envoys to thank its conqueror, a humbling start
quod cum iis pacem fecissent: they thank Rome for granting peace, as if the victor had done them a favour
ob eamque rem corona aurea eos donarent: the golden crown shows a defeated city eager to please Rome
simulque peterent, ut obsides eorum Fregellis essent captivique redderentur: the requests come only after the thanks and the gift, which presents Carthage as a supplicant
munus eorum gratum acceptumque esse; obsides, quo loco rogarent, futuros: Rome’s gracious tone is that of a superior granting favours
captivos non remissuros: the blunt refusal at the end of the reply shows Carthage cannot even recover its own men

hoc responso Carthaginienses cognito Hannibalem domum et Magonem revocarunt: the Carthaginians are enclosed in the ablative absolute of Rome’s reply and act on it at once, a city ruled by Rome’s wishes

ut enim Romae consules, sic Carthagine quotannis annui bini reges creabantur: even Carthage’s own constitution is explained through Rome’s in the balanced ut … sic, so Rome is the measure of everything

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s fall from power in Carthage seem unjust?
points: Hannibal serves as magistrate with the same energy he showed in war
he puts the finances in order: enough to pay Rome and a surplus for the treasury
Roman envoys arrive in Carthage
Hannibal believes they have come to demand his surrender
he flees in secret before they can even be heard
the Carthaginians hunt him with two ships, seize his property and tear down his house
the man who has just filled the treasury is declared an exile by his own city
features: pari diligentia se Hannibal praebuit, ac fuerat in bello: the comparison with his conduct in war presents him as a model magistrate, which makes his fall seem undeserved
non solum ut esset pecunia … sed etiam superesset: the climactic non solum … sed etiam and the echo esset … superesset stress how well he served the state
quae in aerario reponeretur: he fills the city’s treasury, a service that sharpens the injustice of what follows
hos Hannibal ratus sui exposcendi gratia missos: the gerundive of purpose spells out his fear of being handed over to Rome by his own city
priusquam iis senatus daretur, navem ascendit clam: he must slip away in secret before the envoys are even heard, a sad flight for a benefactor
Poeni naves duas, quae eum comprehenderent, si possent consequi, miserunt: the hostile Roman name Poeni is used just as the city hunts down its own hero
miserunt, bona eius publicarunt, domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt: four punishments in asyndeton make the city’s response relentless and excessive
domum a fundamentis disiecerunt: tearing his house down to its foundations is a vindictive act out of all proportion
ipsum exulem iudicarunt: the climax: the man who has just saved the treasury is condemned as an exile, with ipsum stressing the man himself

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s qualities as a statesman and as a man under threat?
points: Hannibal brings the same energy to his office that he showed in war
he is a careful and hard-working magistrate
his reforms produce enough money to pay Rome and a surplus for the treasury
he reads the danger quickly when the Roman envoys arrive
he acts decisively, leaving before the envoys can even address the senate
he escapes in secret and goes straight to Antiochus
the harsh response of the Carthaginians makes his service to the city seem badly rewarded
features: in eo magistratu pari diligentia se Hannibal praebuit, ac fuerat in bello: the comparison shows his talents extend from war to government
namque effecit ex novis vectigalibus: effecit stresses achievement, and the new revenues show his practical skill with finance
non solum ut esset pecunia … sed etiam superesset: the climax and the polyptoton esset … superesset show him producing enough and more than enough
quae Romanis ex foedere penderetur: irony: Rome’s greatest enemy makes sure the treaty payments to Rome are met, a sign of responsible statesmanship
Roma legati Carthaginem venerunt: the envoys are placed between the names of the two cities, so the threat from Rome is seen closing in on Carthage
hos Hannibal ratus sui exposcendi gratia missos: he reads the danger at once, and the gerundive spells out exactly what he fears
priusquam iis senatus daretur, navem ascendit clam atque in Syriam ad Antiochum profugit: the rapid sequence of verbs and clam show decisive, secret action under threat
domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt: the asyndeton of punishments shows how real the threat to him was

essays.q: how does Nepos present the way Carthage treated Hannibal and his family?
points: envoys from Rome come to Carthage
Hannibal expects to be handed over and has to flee in secret
the Carthaginians try to catch him with two ships
they take his property, destroy his house and declare him an exile
the punishments come one after another, which makes the city seem relentless
even in exile Hannibal tries to draw Carthage into Antiochus’ war
his brother Mago is condemned in his absence, exactly as Hannibal was
features: Roma legati Carthaginem venerunt: Rome’s envoys stand between the names of the two cities, so Carthage is seen acting under Roman pressure
hos Hannibal ratus sui exposcendi gratia missos: he expects his own city to hand him over, which shows how little he can trust it
navem ascendit clam atque in Syriam ad Antiochum profugit: the great general has to slip away in secret, which shows how dangerous Carthage has become for him
Poeni naves duas, quae eum comprehenderent, si possent consequi, miserunt: the hostile name Poeni and the verb held back to the end describe a city hunting down its own hero
bona eius publicarunt, domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt: three punishments in asyndeton, rising to exile, make the treatment harsh and relentless
domum a fundamentis disiecerunt: destroying his house to its foundations wipes out the family’s place in the city
cum quinque navibus Africam accessit: the tiny force shows how far the city’s treatment has reduced him
Magonem eadem, qua fratrem, absentem affecerunt poena: the parallel treatment and absentem show the whole family condemned without a hearing

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s loyalty and ability in difficult circumstances?
points: the brothers’ situation is hopeless and they set sail, leaving themselves to fortune
Mago dies an obscure death, by shipwreck or at the hands of his own slaves
Nepos claims that Antiochus would have fought near Rome itself if he had followed Hannibal’s advice
so Hannibal’s strategy is shown to be sound, and the failure is the king’s
Hannibal stays loyal even though he sees the king’s many foolish schemes
he is given only a few ships
even when his side is beaten by numbers, he wins on his own wing
features: illi desperatis rebus cum solvissent naves ac vela ventis dedissent: the ablative absolute and the alliterative vela ventis show how hopeless his circumstances are when he arrives
si tam in gerendo bello consiliis eius parere voluisset, quam in suscipiendo instituerat: the balanced gerunds show his advice was sound, so the failure is the king’s
propius Tiberi quam in Thermopylis de summa imperii dimicasset: the antithesis of Rome’s own river and distant Thermopylae shows how dangerous his strategy would have been to Rome
quem etsi multa stulte conari videbat, tamen nulla deseruit in re: the antithesis of multa and nulla, with etsi … tamen, stresses his loyalty to a foolish king
praefuit paucis navibus: he is given only a few ships, a small command that he still accepts
quo cum multitudine adversariorum sui superarentur: the enemy’s numbers explain the defeat of his side
ipse, quo cornu rem gessit, fuit superior: ipse and superior at the end of the sentence stress his personal success within a lost battle

essays.q: how does Nepos make the situation of Hannibal and his brother seem desperate?
points: Hannibal now has only five ships
he still hopes to bring Carthage into the war against Rome
he has already persuaded Antiochus to send armies to Italy
the Carthaginians punish Mago in his absence, just as they punished Hannibal
the brothers’ position is hopeless and they have to sail away
Mago dies, either in a shipwreck or at the hands of his own slaves
Nepos gives both accounts, so Mago’s end remains uncertain and inglorious
features: anno tertio postquam domo profugerat: the time phrase stresses his long years of exile from home
cum quinque navibus Africam accessit: the tiny force shows how far he has fallen
si forte Carthaginienses ad bellum Antiochi spe fiduciaque inducere posset: si forte (‘in the hope that perhaps’) shows how uncertain his hopes now are
Magonem eadem, qua fratrem, absentem affecerunt poena: Carthage condemns Mago too, in his absence, so both brothers are cut off from home
illi desperatis rebus: the ablative absolute states plainly that their situation is hopeless
cum solvissent naves ac vela ventis dedissent: the poetic phrase, with alliteration of v, pictures the brothers giving themselves up to the winds and to fortune
de Magonis interitu duplex memoria prodita est: Mago’s death is so obscure that even its manner is uncertain
alii naufragio, alii a servulis ipsius interfectum eum: the balanced alii … alii offers two grim ends, and the contemptuous diminutive servulis makes his death humiliating

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a better leader than the king he served?
points: Antiochus took Hannibal’s advice in starting the war but ignored it in fighting it
Nepos claims that with Hannibal’s advice the war would have been fought near Rome
Antiochus is shown attempting many foolish things
Hannibal stays loyal to him in every matter
Antiochus gives Hannibal only a few ships
in the battle against Rhodes the king’s side is beaten by numbers
Hannibal wins on his own wing
features: si tam in gerendo bello consiliis eius parere voluisset, quam in suscipiendo instituerat: the balanced tam … quam shows the king abandoning advice he had first followed
consiliis eius parere: the king ‘obeying’ Hannibal’s counsel reverses their positions and makes Hannibal the true leader
propius Tiberi quam in Thermopylis de summa imperii dimicasset: the antithesis shows what Hannibal’s strategy would have achieved compared with the king’s
quem etsi multa stulte conari videbat: the adverb stulte condemns the king’s schemes, which Hannibal sees through
tamen nulla deseruit in re: the contrast of nulla with multa shows Hannibal’s loyalty and sense of duty outclassing the king’s judgement
praefuit paucis navibus, quas ex Syria iussus erat in Asiam ducere: iussus erat shows the great general taking orders and given only a few ships, so the king wastes his talent
quo cum multitudine adversariorum sui superarentur, ipse, quo cornu rem gessit, fuit superior: his side is beaten while ipse … fuit superior shows that where Hannibal led, he won

essays.q: how does Nepos make the story of Hannibal’s trick entertaining?
points: Hannibal is introduced as the shrewdest of all men, so the reader expects a clever trick
the Cretans are defined by their greed, so the reader enjoys seeing them outwitted
the trick is simple and clever: jars of lead topped with gold and silver
he deposits them in a temple before the leading citizens, pretending to trust their honesty
his real money is hidden in bronze statues and left lying carelessly in the open
the comic reversal: the Cretans guard the temple against Hannibal himself
the reader knows they are guarding lead while the treasure lies in full view
features: vir omnium callidissimus: the superlative introduces Hannibal as the cleverest of all men, so the reader expects a clever trick
propter avaritiam Cretensium: the Cretans are defined by their greed, which makes them targets the reader will enjoy seeing outwitted
itaque capit tale consilium: the short sentence in the historic present builds anticipation, with tale pointing forward to the trick

amphoras complures complet plumbo, summas operit auro et argento: asyndeton and vivid historic presents make the deception quick and concrete, and the alliteration of complures complet adds a playful tone
has praesentibus principibus deponit in templo Dianae: the alliteration of p and the solemn setting of a temple heighten the comedy of the leading men witnessing a sham
simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere: simulans lets the reader in on the pretence and the irony of trusting the ‘good faith’ of greedy men
statuas aeneas, quas secum portabat, omni sua pecunia complet easque in propatulo domi abicit: the real treasure is tossed carelessly into the open courtyard, and abicit makes the bluff audacious
Gortynii templum magna cura custodiunt non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale: comic reversal: non tam … quam shows them guarding the temple above all against the man who deposited the ‘treasure’
ne ille inscientibus iis tolleret sua secumque duceret: the irony is complete: they fear he will secretly take back what is only lead, while his money lies in full view

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a man who thinks ahead?
points: after Antiochus’ defeat Hannibal foresees that he will be handed over
Nepos confirms that this would certainly have happened
he goes to Crete to consider his next move
he sees the danger from the greedy Cretans before it arises
he knows that word of his money has spread
he devises a plan at once and carries it out step by step
he makes the leading citizens witnesses, so they believe his money is in the temple
features: Antiocho fugato verens ne dederetur: he anticipates being handed over the moment Antiochus is defeated
quod sine dubio accidisset, si sui fecisset potestatem: Nepos’ comment sine dubio confirms that his foresight was justified
ut ibi, quo se conferret, consideraret: the purpose clause shows him using Crete as a place to plan his next move
vir omnium callidissimus: the superlative presents him as the shrewdest of all men
in magno se fore periculo, nisi quid providisset: the future infinitive fore shows him predicting danger, and providisset (‘foreseen’) names his foresight
de qua sciebat exisse famam: sciebat shows he knows the rumour has spread before it can be used against him
itaque capit tale consilium: the short sentence in the historic present marks quick, decisive planning
amphoras complures complet plumbo, summas operit auro et argento: the precise steps in asyndeton show a carefully prepared plan
has praesentibus principibus deponit in templo Dianae, simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere: he makes the leading men witnesses, foreseeing exactly how they will react

essays.q: how does Nepos present the Cretans in this episode?
points: the Cretans are defined by their greed from the start
Hannibal fears them because word of his money has spread
their leading men are made witnesses to the deposit in the temple
Hannibal pretends to trust their good faith
they are completely deceived
they guard the temple with great care
they guard it against the very man who deposited the treasure, while his real money lies in his courtyard
features: propter avaritiam Cretensium: the Cretans are introduced through their greed, the trait that defines them in the episode
magnam enim secum pecuniam portabat, de qua sciebat exisse famam: the rumour of his wealth has spread among them, which shows how alert they are to money
has praesentibus principibus deponit in templo Dianae: their leading men are made witnesses, so the whole ruling class is drawn into the deception
simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere: the irony of Hannibal pretending to trust the ‘good faith’ of greedy men exposes them
his in errorem inductis: the brief ablative absolute states that they are completely deceived
Gortynii templum magna cura custodiunt: magna cura shows their anxious greed, devoting great care to jars of lead
non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale: non tam … quam shows them most suspicious of the very man whose money they think they hold, which makes them absurd
ne ille inscientibus iis tolleret sua secumque duceret: their fear of losing what was never theirs makes them look both greedy and foolish

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as an enemy of Rome who never gives up?
points: Hannibal arrives at Prusias’ court fresh from tricking the Cretans, his fortune intact
even in exile his attitude to Italy is unchanged
he does nothing else but arm and train the king against Rome
he sees Prusias is too weak alone, so he builds a wider alliance of kings and warlike peoples
Eumenes is Rome’s close friend, so the war with Prusias becomes a war against Rome’s side
Rome’s alliance gives Eumenes the advantage on land and sea, which only makes Hannibal more determined
he reasons coolly that removing Eumenes will make the rest easier, and plans to kill him
features: sic conservatis suis rebus Poenus illusis Cretensibus omnibus: two ablative absolutes show him arriving with his fortune safe and his enemies outwitted, and Poenus stresses his Carthaginian identity
apud quem eodem animo fuit erga Italiam: eodem animo stresses that his hostility to Rome is unchanged by exile
neque aliud quicquam egit quam regem armavit et exercuit adversus Romanos: neque aliud quicquam … quam shows single-minded devotion, with adversus Romanos placed last for emphasis
quem cum videret domesticis opibus minus esse robustum: he assesses the king’s weakness realistically and adapts his plans
conciliabat ceteros reges, adiungebat bellicosas nationes: asyndeton and the imperfect tenses convey tireless, continuous effort
Pergamenus rex Eumenes, Romanis amicissimus: the superlative marks Eumenes as Rome’s proxy, so Hannibal’s war is still a war against Rome
sed utrobique Eumenes plus valebat propter Romanorum societatem: the obstacle is Rome’s alliance, which explains why Hannibal will not let it rest
quo magis cupiebat eum Hannibal opprimi: quo magis shows that setbacks only make him more determined
ad hunc interficiundum talem iniit rationem: the passage ends on a new plan, so he is always looking for the next way to fight

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s skill as a strategist and diplomat?
points: he has saved his fortune and outwitted every Cretan
at Prusias’ court he works single-mindedly against Rome
he arms and trains the king
he sees that Prusias is too weak on his own
he wins over other kings and warlike nations
he identifies Eumenes, Rome’s ally, as the key enemy
he reasons that removing Eumenes will make everything else easier, and devises a plan
features: sic conservatis suis rebus Poenus illusis Cretensibus omnibus: two ablative absolutes sum up his success in saving his fortune and outwitting every Cretan
regem armavit et exercuit adversus Romanos: the paired verbs show practical military work as he arms and trains the king
quem cum videret domesticis opibus minus esse robustum: videret shows his clear-sighted assessment of the king’s resources
conciliabat ceteros reges, adiungebat bellicosas nationes: matching clauses in asyndeton show his diplomacy in building alliances, and bellicosas shows he chooses useful allies
Pergamenus rex Eumenes, Romanis amicissimus: the superlative identifies Eumenes as Rome’s closest friend and so the key enemy
bellumque inter eos gerebatur et mari et terra: et … et shows the scale of the war he must plan for
quem si removisset, faciliora sibi cetera fore arbitrabatur: the conditional and arbitrabatur show cool strategic reasoning: removing one man unlocks everything else
ad hunc interficiundum talem iniit rationem: talem points forward to a cunning plan, so the passage ends on his inventiveness

essays.q: how does Nepos build up to Hannibal’s unusual plan against Eumenes?
points: Eumenes is at war with Prusias on land and sea
Eumenes is stronger on both fronts because of his alliance with Rome
this makes Hannibal all the more determined to crush him
Hannibal reasons that removing Eumenes is the key to everything else
a sea battle is only days away and Hannibal is outnumbered in ships
since he cannot match the enemy in arms, he must fight by trickery
the order to collect live venomous snakes in clay pots is a surprising and memorable climax
features: dissidebat ab eo Pergamenus rex Eumenes, Romanis amicissimus: the enemy is introduced with Rome’s backing, which raises the stakes
bellumque inter eos gerebatur et mari et terra; sed utrobique Eumenes plus valebat: et … et and utrobique show Eumenes stronger everywhere, so ordinary methods cannot work
quo magis cupiebat eum Hannibal opprimi: quo magis builds Hannibal’s determination in step with the difficulty
quem si removisset, faciliora sibi cetera fore arbitrabatur: his reasoning narrows the problem to one man and focuses the reader on the coming plan
ad hunc interficiundum talem iniit rationem: talem points forward and creates suspense about what the plan will be
classe paucis diebus erant decreturi: the short sentence sets a deadline, which adds urgency

superabatur navium multitudine: dolo erat pugnandum, cum par non esset armis: short clauses in asyndeton state the problem starkly; dolo placed first and the gerundive of obligation show trickery forced on him
imperavit quam plurimas venenatas serpentes vivas colligi: the build-up ends in a startling order, with the adjectives venenatas and vivas piling up the danger
easque in vasa fictilia conici: the homely clay pots make the climax unusual and memorable

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s preparations for the sea battle interesting?
points: the battle is only days away, which creates urgency
Hannibal is outnumbered and outmatched, so the reader wonders how he can win
he turns to trickery as a necessity
the weapon is extraordinary: as many live, venomous snakes as possible, packed into clay pots
the plan is revealed to the marines only on the day of the battle
the orders are simple and clear: all attack the king’s ship and only defend against the rest
Hannibal is confident of easy success and promises a great reward for taking or killing Eumenes
features: classe paucis diebus erant decreturi: the time phrase sets a deadline only days away, so the preparations that follow carry real urgency
superabatur navium multitudine: the verb placed first states Hannibal’s disadvantage bluntly, so the reader is curious to see how he can possibly win

dolo erat pugnandum, cum par non esset armis: the gerundive of obligation and the contrast of dolo with armis turn the problem into a puzzle: trickery is his only weapon, and the reader waits to see what it will be
quam plurimas venenatas serpentes vivas: the superlative and the piling up of adjectives (venomous, alive) make the strange weapon startling and grimly memorable
in vasa fictilia conici: the homely detail of cheap clay pots contrasts with their deadly contents, which makes the plan surprising
multitudine … magnam multitudinem … serpentium multitudine: polyptoton of multitudo shows Hannibal answering the enemy’s multitude of ships with a multitude of snakes, a neat and witty reversal
die ipso, quo facturus erat navale proelium, classiarios convocat: emphatic ipso and the vivid historic present convocat bring the reader into the briefing at the last possible moment
omnes ut in unam Eumenis regis concurrant navem: juxtaposition of omnes and unam, with unam … navem framing the king’s name, makes the single target of the bold plan stand out
id illos facile serpentium multitudine consecuturos: facile in Hannibal’s reported words shows a confidence that makes the reader eager to see whether the plan will work
quem si aut cepissent aut interfecissent, magno iis pollicetur praemio fore: aut … aut and the hyperbaton of magno … praemio raise the stakes, ending the briefing on the promise of a great reward

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a confident and resourceful commander?
points: he faces a clear disadvantage, outnumbered in ships and weaker in arms
he turns at once to cunning, which Nepos presents as a necessity
he devises a strange new weapon: live venomous snakes in clay pots
he prepares on a large scale, collecting as many snakes as possible
he keeps the plan to himself until the very day of the battle
his orders are simple and clear: every ship against Eumenes, mere defence against the rest
he is sure the snakes will make it easy and promises a great reward
features: superabatur navium multitudine: the verb comes first, so Hannibal’s disadvantage is stated plainly before he shows how he will overcome it

dolo erat pugnandum, cum par non esset armis: the gerundive of obligation presents his decision as a clear-headed response to necessity, and the contrast of dolo with armis shows him turning weakness into a plan
imperavit quam plurimas venenatas serpentes vivas colligi: the decisive imperavit and the superlative quam plurimas show a commander who acts on a large scale and does nothing by halves
in vasa fictilia conici: ordinary clay pots become a weapon, which shows his resourcefulness in making use of the simplest materials
die ipso, quo facturus erat navale proelium: emphatic ipso shows his control of timing: he keeps the plan secret until the very day of the battle
classiarios convocat hisque praecepit: the brisk pair of verbs, with the historic present convocat, presents him calmly taking charge of his men

omnes ut in unam Eumenis regis concurrant navem; a ceteris tantum satis habeant se defendere: the balanced contrast of omnes … unam with a ceteris tantum makes his orders simple, clear and easy to follow
id illos facile serpentium multitudine consecuturos: facile conveys his complete confidence in the outcome
rex autem in qua nave veheretur, ut scirent, se facturum: he promises to solve the remaining problem himself, which shows a commander who has thought of everything
quem si aut cepissent aut interfecissent, magno iis pollicetur praemio fore: aut … aut and the great reward show him motivating his men and determined to remove Eumenes by any means

essays.lemma: imperavit quam plurimas … quo loco Eumenes esset
essays.q: how does Nepos build up suspense as the sea battle approaches?
points: the strange order to collect live venomous snakes makes the reader wonder how they will be used
the snakes are packed into ordinary clay pots, so their purpose stays hidden
the plan is revealed to the marines only on the day of the battle
the orders focus everything on one target, King Eumenes
Hannibal promises to show his men where the king is, without saying how
the reward for capturing or killing Eumenes raises the stakes
the fleets are drawn up, and the battle is held back while Hannibal sends his messenger
features: imperavit quam plurimas venenatas serpentes vivas colligi: the strange order, with its pile of adjectives, raises a question the passage does not yet answer: what are the snakes for?
easque in vasa fictilia conici: the snakes vanish into ordinary clay pots, so their purpose stays hidden from the enemy and partly from the reader
die ipso, quo facturus erat navale proelium: emphatic ipso holds the briefing back until the very day of the battle, so the tension rises as time runs out
omnes ut in unam Eumenis regis concurrant navem: the juxtaposition of omnes and unam focuses everything on one target, so the reader waits to see the king’s ship found
rex autem in qua nave veheretur, ut scirent, se facturum: Hannibal promises to show his men the king’s ship without saying how, which leaves the reader in suspense
quem si aut cepissent aut interfecissent, magno iis pollicetur praemio fore: aut … aut and the delayed praemio raise the stakes on the eve of the battle
